summary: Describes a protocol for carrying accounting information between a network access server and a shared accounting server. This is informational, and it was replaced by RFC 2139.

eli5.summary: The front desk writes down how long each visitor stayed and sends the log to a central office for billing.

questions: how to track network usage with radius
subtitle: How to track who logged in, how long they stayed, and how much data they used.

tldr.problem: Internet Service Providers and network operators needed to track user sessions and data usage for billing and management, but had no standard protocol for sending this accounting information from network access servers to a central accounting system.
tldr.mechanism: RADIUS Accounting extends the RADIUS protocol with a simple client-server model where a Network Access Server (NAS) sends accounting records to an accounting server using UDP port 1813, with MD5-based authentication and extensible attribute-value fields.
tldr.outcome: The protocol became a standard way to implement usage-based billing and session tracking for dial-up internet access and other network services. It was replaced by RFC 2139 with enhancements.

today: RFC 2059 was replaced by RFC 2139 with enhancements to the RADIUS Accounting protocol. However, the core protocol and attributes described here remain the basis for network access accounting and session tracking in ISP and enterprise environments.

sections.title: Background and Purpose
sections.content:
RADIUS (Remote Authentication Dial In User Service) was originally designed to handle authentication and authorization for dial-in users. The RFC extends RADIUS to carry accounting information from a Network Access Server (NAS) to a RADIUS accounting server. This allows operators to track user sessions and data usage for billing and resource management.

Key features of RADIUS Accounting include a simple client-server model, network security through shared secrets (rather than passwords sent over the network), and an extensible protocol using variable-length attribute-value tuples so new accounting metrics can be added without breaking existing implementations.
sections.eli5: When someone connects to an internet service, the access machine (NAS) records what happened: when they logged in, when they logged out, how much data they used. This RFC describes how to send those records to a central office for billing.

sections.title: Basic Accounting Flow
sections.content:
When a user connects to a NAS and starts receiving service, the NAS generates an Accounting Start packet and sends it to the RADIUS accounting server, which sends back an acknowledgement. When the user disconnects, the NAS generates an Accounting Stop packet with statistics such as elapsed time, input octets (bytes received), and output octets (bytes sent), and the server acknowledges receipt.

The client should continue trying to send accounting requests until it receives an acknowledgement, using some form of backoff if the server does not respond. If no response arrives within a time limit, the request is retransmitted multiple times. The client can forward requests to alternate accounting servers if the primary server is down or unreachable.
sections.eli5: When someone logs in, the NAS sends a message saying "person X is starting." When they log out, it sends another message saying "person X used Y hours and downloaded Z megabytes." If the accounting server does not say OK, the NAS keeps trying until it gets through.

sections.title: Packet Format and Structure
sections.content:
RADIUS Accounting packets are encapsulated in UDP with destination port 1813. Each packet contains four main parts: a Code field (one octet) identifying the packet type, an Identifier field (one octet) to match requests and replies, a Length field (two octets) indicating total packet size, and a 16-octet Authenticator field containing an MD5 hash for security.

The Request Authenticator in an Accounting-Request contains an MD5 hash calculated from the packet contents plus a shared secret (never sent over the network). The Response Authenticator in an Accounting-Response is an MD5 hash of the response code, identifier, length, the original request authenticator, any response attributes, and the shared secret.
sections.eli5: Each message is a small packet with a header saying what kind of message it is, a number to match the answer, the total size, and a secret fingerprint so both sides know the message is real.

sections.title: Accounting-Request and Accounting-Response
sections.content:
Accounting-Request packets (Code 4) are sent from a NAS to an accounting server. The server MUST send an Accounting-Response (Code 5) if it successfully records the packet, and MUST NOT send any reply if recording fails. An Accounting-Request must contain either a NAS-IP-Address or NAS-Identifier attribute, and optionally NAS-Port information.

Certain attributes MUST NOT appear in an Accounting-Request: User-Password, CHAP-Password, Reply-Message, and State. The request can include any other valid RADIUS attributes to describe the user and service. An Accounting-Response does not require any attributes and can be empty except for the authenticator.
sections.eli5: The NAS sends a request saying "here is what happened." If the accounting server successfully writes it down, it sends back "OK, I got it." If something goes wrong at the server, it does not say anything (stays silent).

sections.title: Accounting Attributes
sections.content:
RADIUS Accounting defines 12 new attribute types (codes 40-51) to carry session information. Acct-Status-Type (40) indicates Start, Stop, Accounting-On or Accounting-Off. Acct-Delay-Time (41) shows how many seconds the NAS has been trying to send the record.

Acct-Input-Octets (42) and Acct-Output-Octets (43) count bytes received and sent during the session. Acct-Session-Id (44) is a unique string matching start and stop records. Acct-Session-Time (46) counts seconds of service. Acct-Terminate-Cause (49) explains why the session ended: user request, lost carrier, idle timeout, admin reset, port error, or other specific reasons.

Additional attributes include Acct-Authentic (45) indicating authentication method (RADIUS, local or remote), Acct-Input-Packets (47) and Acct-Output-Packets (48) for packet counts, Acct-Multi-Session-Id (50) linking related sessions, and Acct-Link-Count (51) for multilink sessions.
sections.eli5: The message includes labeled fields like "session started", "session stopped", "bytes downloaded", "bytes uploaded", "how long the session lasted", and "why it ended". Each field has a number so both sides know what information they are talking about.

sections.title: Session Termination and Multilink Support
sections.content:
Acct-Terminate-Cause values describe how and why a session ended. Common causes include: User Request (user logged out), Lost Carrier (connection dropped), Idle Timeout (user inactive), Session Timeout (maximum time exceeded), Admin Reset (administrator ended it), Admin Reboot (NAS shutting down), Port Error, NAS Error, and others.

For multilink sessions (multiple connections from one user), Acct-Multi-Session-Id links related sessions while each session gets a unique Acct-Session-Id. Acct-Link-Count tracks how many links are in the multilink group at the time of the record, helping accounting servers detect when all parts of a multilink session have been received.
sections.eli5: When someone logs out, the NAS explains why: maybe they typed logout, maybe the connection dropped, maybe they were idle too long, maybe the administrator kicked them off. For people with multiple connections at once, all their connections get the same group ID but each has its own session ID.
